original_question: Prove that the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equation admits wandering solutions.
target_in_paper: Section 11, Problem 30: "Prove that the 3D Euler equation has wandering solutions." The sentence immediately before it says this is the unknown 3D analogue of Nadirashvili’s 2D annulus example of wandering behavior. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the exact target almost verbatim: it is about the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equation and asks for wandering solutions, exactly the content of Problem 30 in the subsection on wandering, chaos, non-mixing, and KAM. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
missing_details: The governing PDE and ambient setup are implicit in your draft. In the paper’s notation, one starts with the incompressible Euler system on a fixed 3D domain M ⊂ R^3, partial_t v + v·∇v = -∇p and div v = 0, with v tangent to ∂M when there is boundary; §1 also records the more general 3D Riemannian-manifold version. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

The term "wandering solutions" is not defined in your draft. The nearby context explains it as an initial condition whose neighborhood never returns sufficiently close after some time; in standard dynamical-systems language, a stand-alone formulation should say that there exist v_0, an open neighborhood U of v_0, and T > 0 such that S_t(U) ∩ U = ∅ for all t > T, where S_t is the Euler evolution in the chosen phase-space topology. This formalization is an explicit unpacking of the paper’s prose. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

The phase space, regularity class, and topology in which U is open are left implicit in Problem 30, and your draft leaves them implicit as well. The surrounding 3D comparison results are quoted in C^k topologies with non-integer k > 4, and a local statement near typical steady states is quoted for non-integer k > 10, but Problem 30 itself does not specify one topology. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

A fully stand-alone version should make clear that this is an existence problem for at least one forward-global 3D Euler orbit with the wandering property, not a universal statement about every solution or every 3-manifold/domain. The official wording is only the existence-type claim that the 3D Euler equation "has wandering solutions." ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
refined_question: In the paper’s basic setup, let M ⊂ R^3 be a fixed fluid domain and consider the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations partial_t v + v·∇v = -∇p and div v = 0, with v tangent to ∂M if ∂M ≠ ∅. Prove that the induced Euler evolution S_t admits a wandering solution: namely, find a forward-global divergence-free initial datum v_0, an open neighborhood U of v_0 in a natural phase space/topology where the Euler flow is defined, and a time T > 0 such that S_t(U) ∩ U = ∅ for every t > T. This is exactly the 3D analogue sought in Problem 30 of the 2D wandering phenomenon mentioned just before it. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
justification: The draft should not be shifted to the broader neighboring KAM question in Problem 31 about relaxing smoothness assumptions for known non-mixing results. The exact paper target is Problem 30 itself. Section 11 first contrasts finite-dimensional Poincaré recurrence with the failure of recurrence in infinite-dimensional Euler dynamics, recalls Nadirashvili’s 2D wandering result, and then asks for the 3D analogue in a single sentence. The refinement therefore keeps the scope narrow and paper-faithful, adding only the notation from §1 and the neighborhood-based meaning of "wandering" that is implicit in the surrounding prose. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
